Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence (basis for Year Established): Acts 17:1-9, Paul's visit c. 49/50 CE (conventional date; c. used). Paul and Silas came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews; Paul argued in it on three Sabbaths; some Jews, many devout Greeks and leading women joined him. Jewish opponents then raised a mob, attacked Jason's house and brought Jason and other believers before the city authorities (politarchs), who took bail and released them. Acts 17:13: Jews of Thessalonica later went to Beroea to stir up crowds against Paul. This points to an organized community with a synagogue and some local influence. No count is given. Not used as rows (no documented presence): claims that Jews first settled c. 168 BCE, c. 140-143 BCE (Alexandrian Jews) or soon after the city's founding in 315 BCE; these are conjectures that later community histories report.

Ovadiah (Tel Aviv Univ.), Gerion 33 (2015): Acts places Jewish communities and synagogues in Philippi, Thessaloniki and Beroea. Paul targeted 'large, famous cities with a flourishing Jewish population, such as Thessaloniki' and met 'sharp opposition from the local Jewish community' (c. 50 CE, Acts 17). Ovadiah also cites Philo, Legatio 281-282 (c. 40 CE), on Jewish colonies in Macedonia, a regional statement that does not name Thessalonica. All material Jewish evidence from the city is later than 74 CE and is therefore not used as rows. It includes the burial inscription of Abramios and his wife Theodote (CIJ I 693, late 2nd c. CE); the sarcophagus of M. Aurelius Iakob alias Eutychios, with a fine payable to 'the synagogues' (c. 3rd c. CE); a menorah-decorated tomb (early Byzantine); and a bilingual Samaritan-Hebrew/Greek synagogue inscription (Samaritans, not counted as Jews). No population figure.

1 Thessalonians, written c. 50-52 CE per scholarly consensus (midpoint 51; c.). In 1 Thess 2:14-16, Paul says the Thessalonian believers suffered from their own compatriots as the Judean churches did from the Jews. Taylor (HTS 58/2, 2002) argues the local Jewish community may have taken part in persecuting the church. Taylor notes that 'the very existence of such a Jewish community is disputed'. He says there is 'no archaeological evidence of a synagogue, and only ambiguous inscriptional evidence for a Jewish population during the first half of the first century CE' (citing Riesner 1998:344-45). He nevertheless concludes, following Wanamaker 1990:4, that it is 'highly likely that a significant Jewish community existed at Thessalonica' at the time of Paul's mission. No count is given.

Named individual: Aristarchus of Thessalonica, companion of Paul. Acts 20:4 (c. 57 CE; c.) lists him among those accompanying Paul. Acts 27:2 (c. 59/60 CE) calls him 'a Macedonian from Thessalonica'. In Colossians 4:10-11 Paul lists Aristarchus, Mark and Jesus Justus as 'the only ones of the circumcision among my coworkers', which is usually read as making Aristarchus a Jew. This is evidence of a Thessalonian Jewish individual, not a community count.

Papanastasopoulou, 'To evraiko nekrotafeio tis Thessalonikis' (paper, Aristotle Univ. Thessaloniki): states that a Jewish community 'flourished' in Thessaloniki around its synagogue, which the apostle Paul visited (Acts 17:1). The text says '1st c. BCE' (1os ai. p.Ch.), but because it is tied to Paul's visit it evidently means the 1st c. CE, so the row is dated c. 50 CE. The paper reports settlement hypotheses of 168 BCE (after the Maccabean revolt), 140-143 BCE (Jews fleeing Alexandria) and shortly after the city's founding in 315 BCE (inferred from Strabo's remark that Jews were everywhere); these are views, not documented presence. It also says the ancient Jewish cemetery (now under the Aristotle University campus) was founded in the early Roman period, but its dated inscriptions (e.g. M. Aurelius Iakob) are 2nd-3rd c. CE or later. No count.
